title: Then It Just Runs
logline: In a coastal village of home weaving sheds, several hundred metres of thread are stretched down a lane, sized, wound onto a beam, and then drawn one end at a time through a heddle eye and a dent in a reed — a few thousand of them, over days — and at the end of all of it the only thing that happens is that a loom starts running the way it ran before, and goes on running, and will have to be set up again in a few weeks.
human_question: If the end of a long preparation turns out to be only that ordinary work can begin, what were we expecting instead?

place.what_kind_of_place: A village of low tiled roofs on a coast road, palmyra and coconut over it, sand lanes between the compounds, and a lagoon behind. The work is not in a factory. It is in sheds and front rooms: a frame loom of hardwood and iron filling most of a room, with a bench, four treadles worn smooth, two beams, a reed in a wooden batten, and a few hundred or a few thousand heddles hanging in their shafts like a comb with every tooth threaded separately. Beside the loom, bobbins on a rack, a hand winder, a bucket of size, a pair of scissors, a hook the thickness of a wire, and a chair for whoever is going to sit there for three days doing nothing but passing thread through holes. And out in the lane, on the mornings when a warp is laid, a line of pegs driven into the sand and several hundred metres of thread walked out between them in parallel — the one part of the process that will not fit indoors. Several houses in the village do this, each with its own looms, its own reeds, its own yarn and its own orders, and none of them is doing quite the same cloth as the one next door.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because the place gives one shot that is also the whole idea and would be beautiful to somebody who never hears a word of it: from directly overhead, a sand lane with several hundred metres of parallel coloured threads stretched down it between pegs, bright and exact against the sand, with two people walking the length of it and the roofs and palms on either side. A laid warp seen from above is a road with every strand of it visible at once, and that is the film. Close, the film is the opposite of spectacular: a bobbin filling; thread walked out and crossed at the far peg; size worked in with a hand; a beam turned tooth by tooth; and then the part nobody films, because it looks like nothing — a person on a low chair for the better part of three days, taking one end of thread at a time, pushing a hook through the eye of a heddle, pulling the end through, and then through one dent of the reed, several thousand times, in an order that cannot be varied. And then, at the very end, the smallest event in the whole group of films: a treadle goes down, a shuttle goes across, and a loom starts making cloth.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The order changes nothing and can be changed by nothing. Every step exists only because of the step before it: no end can go through a reed before it has gone through a heddle, nothing can be wound before it is sized, nothing can be drawn before it is wound. Once the threading is done, the character of the cloth is already fixed — its width, its density, its pattern repeat — and no amount of skill at the bench afterwards can alter it. What happens on the day the loom is tied in is that everything stops being preparation. And then the change stops: the loom runs at the same rate, in the same way, for as many weeks as the warp lasts, and the only thing that moves is the diameter of the beam getting smaller. When it runs out, all of it is done again from the beginning, with a different reed or the same one.
place.when_it_looks_best: The warp in the lane wants the first two hours of a dry, still morning, when the threads take a long shadow and read from directly above; that is the shot the film is built on, it happens only on the mornings a warp is laid, and it cannot be arranged. The threading wants the flat middle of the day indoors, in whatever light the shed has, filmed long and without cuts, because its whole quality is duration. The tying-in and the first picks want to be taken whenever they happen. The last hour is for the village from height with looms audible under the roofs, and for the loom itself, running, with nobody watching it.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A film about setting a loom up. Bobbins filling on a hand winder; several hundred metres of thread walked out between pegs down a sand lane and crossed at the far end; size worked in; a beam wound tooth by tooth; a person on a low chair for three days passing one end of thread at a time through the eye of a heddle and a dent in a reed; the old ends knotted to the new in bunches and pulled through; a beam tensioned; a treadle down, a shuttle across, and the first rough inches of cloth held up against the light and read for mistakes. Then a room in which a loom is simply running, and a warp beam that is slightly smaller than it was this morning. It has a complete shape with nothing said over it, and anyone who likes exact hand work, or the fact that a cloth is decided before it is woven, has a whole piece here.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same week becomes the largest map the series has used and the plainest thing at the end of it. The sources lay the road out as seven successive purifications, beginning not with any inner experience but with ordinary conduct, and they give a practical rather than a moral reason for that order. They insist throughout that clarity comes from repetition and not from any single insight, and their images for it are domestic: wipe the mirror again, press the sesame again, stir the clearing seeds again until the mud settles. They match the object of practice to the person and they say plainly that each object has a ceiling it cannot pass. They warn that the moment practice starts going well is the dangerous one, because that is when a person decides they have arrived. And at the end of hundreds of pages they leave laypeople with almost nothing: keep your own commitments, and take them up again, and again. A loom being set up carries all of that in the only order it can be done in, and the film's last statement is the smallest one available: after everything, the ordinary resumes, and will need setting up again. The voice says, once and without decoration, that the decisive change the map ends in has the unconditioned for its object, and that this is the one thing in a hundred films that cannot be shown.

sequence.on_screen: First light, straight down over a sand lane between compounds. Several hundred metres of parallel coloured threads stretched between pegs the length of it, bright and exact against the sand, with two people walking the line. Tiled roofs, palmyra and coconut on either side. Held very long.
sequence.voice: This is the last of these films, and the largest map in the sources is the one it has to use. They set the road out as seven purifications in a fixed order, and the order is the whole point: nothing in it can be reached before the thing before it. What is stretched down this lane is a few days of work that has to happen before any cloth exists, and it is already, this morning, the exact width, density and pattern of cloth that will come off the loom in a month.

sequence.on_screen: The steps in their order, at working length. A bobbin filling on a hand winder. Thread walked out between the pegs and crossed at the far end. Size worked in along the length of it with a hand. The beam turned tooth by tooth while somebody holds the tension. Then a person on a low chair with a wire hook, taking one end at a time through the eye of a heddle and then through one dent of the reed. Again. Again.
sequence.voice: The sources are unusually plain about how this kind of clarity comes, and it is not by any single insight. Their images for it are household ones. When one or two pressings give no oil, sprinkle hot water on the sesame meal and press it again [C097-P4:L1154]. When the water stays muddy, stir the clearing seeds round the pot again until the mud goes down [C097-P4:L1156–L1162]. When it stalls, they do not ask for a breakthrough. They ask for steadier attention, a suitable place, and not breaking off between one session and the next.

sequence.on_screen: Before any of that, and shown out of sequence, the loom itself being made ready. Wedges tapped under the frame until it stands level. The treadles tried. The bench set. The floor swept and the shed's one window unshuttered. Nothing being made.
sequence.voice: The map's first stage is conduct, and the reason the sources give for putting it first is practical rather than moral. Clean conduct leaves nothing to be ashamed of; a mind with nothing to be ashamed of becomes glad; gladness becomes joy; joy becomes calm; and calm is what makes steady attention possible at all [C097-P4:L819–L859]. It is the floor the rest stands on and it is not the goal. A loom that is not level does not make bad cloth later. It makes no cloth.

sequence.on_screen: Four sheds in the same village in one sequence: four looms, four reeds of different counts, four different yarns and setts and patterns, four different people at them, nobody doing the same thing as the house next door. Then one reed held up close, and the dents counted along an inch of it.
sequence.voice: For settling the mind the sources give forty subjects in seven groups, and two rules about them. They are matched to the person — to temperament, to what pulls at them — and taken from a teacher rather than chosen off a list [C085-P:L47; C085-P4:L61]. And each one has a ceiling it cannot pass: some can carry a mind all the way into absorption, and some, however long anybody works at them, only ever bring it to the doorway [C085-P4:L307]. The loom's version of that is in the hand: the count of dents to the inch in this reed fixes the finest cloth this loom can make, whoever sits at it.

sequence.on_screen: The tying-in. The last ends of the finished warp still standing in the heddles; the new ends laid against them and knotted in small bunches; the knots drawn through the reed a handful at a time; the beam tensioned. Then a treadle down, a shuttle across, and the first inches of cloth, visibly rough.
sequence.voice: For the change at the end of the road the sources use one image twice. A man runs at a canal, takes hold of a rope hanging from a branch, swings out over the water, lets go, lands on the far bank shaking, and only after that finds his footing [C100-P4:L44–L46; C100-P:L83]. They give arriving and being settled to two different moments on purpose, and they say the unsteadiness just afterwards is part of the process and not a sign that it failed. The first hand's width of cloth off a new warp is always poor. Nobody in this room regards that as a problem.

sequence.on_screen: The first metre cut off at the edge and held up against the window. A crossed end found and traced back. Two threads discovered in one heddle eye. A missed dent. The fault opened up and corrected. Then a short list of the things that are wrong and are going to stay wrong for the whole warp, said aloud and accepted.
sequence.voice: And after the change the sources put a review, five things looked back over: the road that was taken, what was gained by it, what is genuinely gone, what is still left, and where the person has actually arrived [C100-P4:L83–L93]. They note that some people skip the two awkward questions in the middle, and that only somebody entirely finished has nothing on the list of what remains. It is an audit and not a celebration. The person best placed to say what is still wrong is the one who did the work.

sequence.on_screen: The loom running steadily. The shuttle going and coming, the batten, the treadles, the cloth growing at a rate that is hard to see. Nobody is watching it. The shed's ordinary noise, a radio somewhere, somebody outside.
sequence.voice: Here is what this film is not. The change the map ends in is not an insight, a realisation or a turning point in anybody's life. The sources describe a fixed order of moments whose object is the unconditioned — the one thing in a hundred of these films that cannot be filmed — and they are firm that the persons named along that road are not levels of personal growth and that slower and quicker are not measures of anybody [C100-P4:L26–L30; C100-P4:L81]. They also warn about exactly this moment, when the work starts going well: light, ease, confidence and sharpness arrive, and the danger is not the good feeling but deciding it is the destination [C097-M:L103–L121; C097-M:L123]. Nothing on this loom is the thing. No shot is.

sequence.on_screen: Last light, from height. The lane where the warp was, empty and swept, with the peg holes still in the sand. Roofs, palms, the lagoon behind. Looms audible under two or three of the roofs. Then, at ground level and last, the loom running, and the warp beam with a visibly smaller diameter than it had this morning.
sequence.voice: At the end of hundreds of pages, what the sources leave people who are not going to leave their households is almost nothing. Keep your own commitments; and when they are broken, mend them and take them up again, and again [C097-P4:L1020–L1022; C097-M:L18]. Not a ladder, not a state, and nothing to be finished. This warp will run out in about a month, and then every one of these steps will be done again from the beginning, in the same order, by the same hands. That is the last thing this series has to say, and it is not a disappointment. A long preparation ends in ordinary work. The ordinary work is what all of it was for.

concept_merge.why_together: C097 is the largest structure the series uses and it supplies both ends of this film. It gives the seven purifications as a fixed order beginning with conduct, and it gives the source's own practical reason for beginning there: clean conduct leaves no remorse, remorse-free gladness becomes joy, joy becomes calm, and calm makes steady attention possible [C097-P4:L819–L859]. It insists repeatedly that progress is repetition rather than revelation, with the sesame press and the clearing-nut seeds as its images [C097-P4:L1154; C097-P4:L1156–L1162]. It warns that light, joy, ease, confidence and sharpness are corruptions the moment they are taken as arrival [C097-M:L103–L121; C097-M:L123]. And it closes its first purification by telling laypeople to keep their own precepts and retake them again and again [C097-P4:L1020–L1022; C097-M:L18], which is the plainest ending available to the whole slate. C100 supplies the decisive moment and, more importantly, the refusal: the crossing is a fixed order of mind-moments whose object is the unconditioned [C100-P4:L26–L30], the canal-and-rope image separates arriving from being settled [C100-P4:L44–L46; C100-P:L83], the five reviewings turn the aftermath into an honest audit including a count of what remains [C100-P4:L83–L93], and the digest is explicit that none of this is an epiphany and that the noble persons are not personal-growth levels [C100-P4:L81]. C085 supplies the variety and the ceiling: forty subjects in seven groups, matched to the person and taken from a teacher rather than chosen [C085-P:L47; C085-P4:L61], each with a limit it cannot pass however long anybody works at it [C085-P4:L307]. Setting up a loom is the one process available to a camera that has all three properties at once: an order that cannot be varied, a ceiling fixed before any work begins, and an ending whose only event is that ordinary work resumes.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the end of the largest map in this tradition is not a summit but a resumption, and that this is the honest way to end a hundred films. Said flat, seven purifications are a diagram and the lay ending is a footnote. Put on a week in which a few thousand threads are passed one at a time through a comb and a reed so that a loom can go back to doing what it was doing before, the diagram becomes a sequence with a deadline and the footnote becomes the last line of the series. The film also gets three of the sources' own guards where the footage can carry them: the ceiling, because a reed's count fixes the finest cloth a loom can make and no skill afterwards can exceed it; the separation of arriving from settling, because the first hand's width of cloth off a new warp is always rough and nobody treats that as failure; and the audit, because a weaver reading the first metre against the light names what is wrong and what will stay wrong for the whole warp. This idea has been round once before. Its first version filmed the last morning of a silent retreat: that is dropped because the slate has already refused filming retreatants, who are there precisely not to be observed, because inner states cannot be filmed and a camera in that room changes the room, and because a group of strangers' first words would inevitably have been read as a shared attainment. The concepts are unchanged. There is no meditator, no retreat and no practice anywhere in this film.

concept_links.why: The film is the shape of the seven purifications, the source's own insistence on repetition, and its lay ending, and nothing else from a very large concept. The practical reason for beginning with conduct is narrated over a loom being levelled before anything is made [C097-P4:L819–L859]. The sesame-press and clearing-nut images are narrated over the plainest and longest stretch of the work [C097-P4:L1154; C097-P4:L1156–L1162]. The warning about light, ease and confidence being corruptions when taken as arrival is narrated at the one moment the film could be mistaken for a triumph [C097-M:L103–L121; C097-M:L123]. And the lay ending closes both the film and the slate [C097-P4:L1020–L1022; C097-M:L18]. Every limit in the digest that bears on this film is honoured. The sequence is not offered as seven steps to wellbeing or inner peace: the film never numbers a beat, never maps a stage onto a task, and the closing beat says outright that there is nothing to be finished [C097-P4:L859]. The four-fold purity is monastic and is not used; no alms, robes, requisites or monastic rule appears, and the film uses only the lay ending the Margaya itself gives. The list of places and households a monk should avoid is not used or alluded to. The stories of monks burned rather than cutting a creeper, and of the broken thigh, are not used. Reflective use of requisites is not turned into a frugality message. The miracle elements in the exemplary stories are not narrated. Impermanence is not used to encourage savouring anything, and relish is named as the trap rather than the reward. The body counts, the decade scheme, the mind-moment timings and the rebirth claims are all left out, and nothing in the film is a verdict on how anybody should feel about their life.

This concept carries the film's decisive beat and its single most important refusal. The canal-and-rope image is narrated over the tying-in and the first rough inches of cloth, with the source's own separation of arriving from being settled [C100-P4:L44–L46; C100-P:L83]. The five reviewings are narrated over a weaver reading the first metre against the light and naming what will stay wrong for the whole warp, including the digest's note that only somebody entirely finished has nothing on that list [C100-P4:L83–L93]. And the seventh beat states the digest's own limits in as many words: the change is a fixed order of mind-moments whose object is the unconditioned, which cannot be filmed [C100-P4:L26–L30], and the persons named on that road are not a ladder of personal-growth levels, with slower and quicker not measuring anybody [C100-P4:L81]. Every limit in the digest is honoured and two of them are spoken. It is not filmed as an aha moment, an epiphany or a life-changing realisation: the film says so directly, over the one shot that could carry that reading. It is not turned into 'let go and move on' self-help, and nothing in the film is about decluttering, leaving anything or ending anything. The irreversibility is not generalised into a claim about big decisions. Fruition attainment is not filmed and not described as a calm state anybody could enter. Reviewing is not presented as journaling or goal-setting. And nobody in the film is presented as having crossed anything: the weavers are doing paid work, and their skill, patience and judgement are not offered as attainments or as echoes of any.

C085 gives the film its one beat about variety and its one hard-edged fact. The digest's two rules are narrated together over four sheds with four different reeds, setts, yarns and patterns: the subject is matched to the person and taken from a teacher rather than chosen from a list [C085-P:L47; C085-P4:L61], and each subject has a ceiling it cannot pass however long anybody works at it, so that some reach absorption and some only ever reach its doorway [C085-P4:L307]. The reed's count is the film's physical form of that ceiling, and the voice says it is the film's analogy rather than the source's. Every limit in the digest is honoured. Nothing here is offered as mindfulness for stress or as a technique: no practice is filmed at all. The corpse and food contemplations are not used, so the digest's warning about reading them as disgust or diet advice does not arise. The recollections of the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha are not used, and neither is the recollection of one's own virtue or giving, so nothing in the film reads as positive thinking or self-congratulation. The promised good rebirth is not used. The father-and-son famine parable is not used. The four elements are not presented as chemistry and the puppet image is not turned into a soul, because neither appears. The particle measures, the cosmology and the supernormal powers are absent, and the butcher simile is not used anywhere.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the largest map in this tradition is a fixed sequence of seven purifications in which nothing can be reached before the thing before it, that it starts with ordinary conduct for a practical rather than a moral reason, and that the sources say clarity comes from repetition rather than from any single insight. That the object a person works with is matched to them and has a ceiling it cannot pass. That the decisive change at the end is described as a fixed order of mind-moments whose object is the unconditioned, which is the one thing in the whole series that cannot be filmed, and that the persons named along that road are not levels of personal growth. That arriving and being settled are given to two different moments, and that what follows a change is an honest audit including a count of what remains. And that what the sources finally leave a layperson with is to keep their commitments and take them up again, and again — so that the end of a long preparation is that ordinary work can begin, and will have to be prepared for again.
what_must_be_real: One real setting-up, in the households' own order and at their own speed, with their agreement, from the morning a warp is actually laid to the day the loom is running. The warp is not laid again for the camera, the threading is not restarted, no end is pulled out and re-threaded for a better angle, the tying-in is not repeated, and the first picks are filmed once. The threading is not compressed into a montage that hides how long it takes, because its duration is the subject. If the setting-up goes wrong — a crossed end that costs a day, a reed of the wrong count, a warp that has to be cut back — the film has that and keeps it. Nobody is named or followed as a character, nobody's patience or steadiness is presented as an attainment or as an echo of one, nobody is asked to confirm or illustrate any doctrine, and nobody is asked what the work means to them. No household's earnings, piece rates, orders, buyers or debts are put on screen, and the film does not become an account of what handloom weaving pays. The sheds are people's homes: the households decide what is filmed indoors, and no interior, name or gate number appears without that. Drone flight over the lane and the compounds happens only with the agreement of the houses it passes over.
position_hint: last in the group and last in the whole slate, and built to be an ending that does not claim anything. It has to follow the film about release, because that one empties something and says the emptiness is not the answer, and this one lets ordinary conditions start up again afterwards. Its final beat is the plainest statement available to the series: that the map's lay ending is to take the commitments up again and again, and that a long preparation ends in ordinary work. It is deliberately the smallest event in the group. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Letting the last film of a hundred reach for a summit. The subject is a resumption, and any swell of arrival in the edit would contradict the one thing the sources say most clearly about this material.
Letting the seven purifications be mapped onto seven tasks, or the beats be numbered, which would turn the largest structure in the series into a diagram and the concept into a ladder.
Compressing the threading into a montage. Its whole content is that it takes three days, and hiding that removes the film's argument.
Implying that any weaver is practising, concentrating in the technical sense, or has attained anything, or that their composure is an echo of the map.
Letting the reed's ceiling become a statement about what people are capable of, rather than about what an object can carry, which is what the digest actually says.
Turning the film into an account of what handloom work pays, or into a piece about a craft in decline, either of which would replace the concept with a livelihood story.
Romanticising home piecework, or making a village's sheds picturesque while its economics are kept off screen.
Letting the aerial of the laid warp be read as a path, a road or a metaphor the sources intended. It is the film's own image and must be named as such if it is named at all.
Intruding on houses. These are homes with looms in them, and the film's most intimate material is somebody's front room.
drop_if: No household will allow a whole setting-up to be followed, from the laying of a warp to the loom running, on their own terms and in their own time.
Warps are no longer laid outdoors here, so the one shot the film is built on does not exist and there is no reason to be in this place rather than any other.
The preparation has moved to a central facility, so the sequence can no longer be followed in one village.
Filming indoors cannot be done without changing how the work is done or exposing households who do not want to be seen.
Height cannot be obtained over the lanes and compounds with the agreement of the houses underneath.

connections.note: That film empties something and says plainly that the emptiness is not the answer; this one lets ordinary conditions start up again afterwards and ends the slate on the resumption rather than on the release.
Two films about a fixed order with a deadline in it: one sets a place down before an absence, the other sets a thing up so that ordinary work can carry on.
Two films about the proportion between preparation and result, from opposite ends: three hours for two seconds there, three days for weeks of unremarkable running here.

selection.reason: It is the one process available to a camera whose order cannot be varied, whose ceiling is fixed before any work begins, and whose only event at the end is that ordinary work resumes — which is exactly the ending the sources' own lay conclusion asks a hundred films to have.

review.note: Rewritten and relocated 2026-09-24. The previous version filmed the last morning of a silent retreat; that is dropped because the slate has already refused filming retreatants, who are there precisely not to be observed, because no inner state can be filmed and a camera in that room would change the room, and because a group of strangers saying their first words would have read as a shared attainment however carefully it was narrated. The concepts are unchanged and all three links are kept, re-grounded and rewritten. The subject is now one setting-up of a handloom in a village of home weaving sheds: the warp laid in a lane, sized, wound, and then a few thousand ends drawn one at a time through a heddle and a reed over about three days, so that at the end the only event is that a loom starts running the way it ran before. There is no meditator, no retreat and no practice anywhere in the film. Because this is the last film of the slate, the ending was written to land on a resumption rather than a summit: the closing beat is the Margaya's own lay conclusion, that commitments are mended and taken up again and again, and the seventh beat says in as many words that the decisive change in the map has the unconditioned for its object and that no shot in a hundred films can be it. Every citation was re-tested against its digest's own evidence before use, and two traps were checked in particular: the C097 Margaya lines about the corruptions of insight resolve as C097-M:L103–L121 with C097-M:L123 and not as a longer run, and the digest's reference to M:L177–L183 has no enclosing evidence range, so that citation is deliberately not used anywhere in this file. C097-P4:L819–L859, C097-P4:L1154, C097-P4:L1156–L1162 and C097-P4:L1020–L1022 are all ranges the digest itself cites. C097's monastic four-fold purity, its list of households a monk should avoid, its self-harm stories and its rebirth claims are all unused; C085's corpse, food and recollection practices are unused; and C100's fruition attainment is not filmed.

suggested_location.name: The home handloom sheds of the coast-road weaving villages south of the district town, around Kattankudy and the Manmunai divisions

also_known_as.name: Palamunai
also_known_as.meaning: a village about thirteen kilometres from the district town that is reported to be heavily engaged in handloom weaving, with much of the work done in people's own homes by both men and women

also_known_as.name: reed, or raachchi
also_known_as.meaning: the comb of flat dents in the batten that spaces the warp and beats the weft home; its count of dents to the inch fixes the finest cloth a loom can make. The local term is reported and not confirmed with anybody in the trade

also_known_as.name: street warping
also_known_as.meaning: laying a warp of several hundred metres between pegs driven into the ground outdoors, because it will not fit inside the shed; the one part of the process that happens in public

suggested_location.region: Batticaloa District, Eastern Province: the coast-road villages south of the district town, between the sea and the lagoon, where handloom weaving is done in homes rather than in a mill
suggested_location.why_here: Because the work is domestic here, several houses in the same village do it, and the one shot the film is built on happens in the open. This district has a working handloom tradition that is not a heritage display: a village a short way down the coast road from the district town is reported to be substantially engaged in it, with both men and women weaving in their own homes and producing sarongs, saris, table linen and small goods, and there are producer groups in the district with names and addresses rather than only artisans in the abstract. That matters for the film in three ways. It means a whole setting-up can be followed in one place, because the winding, the warping, the sizing, the beaming, the threading, the tying-in and the weaving all happen within a few compounds of each other. It means several looms with different reeds, setts, yarns and patterns are within walking distance, which is the one beat the film needs for the variety and the ceiling. And it means the warp is laid outdoors, in a sand lane between houses, which gives the film its single most beautiful frame and its clearest statement in the same shot: several hundred metres of parallel thread seen from directly above. The film also needs a place where nothing is spectacular, because its subject is the smallest event in the group, and a village of low roofs with looms audible under two or three of them is exactly that.
what_to_film: The laid warp from directly overhead in the first two hours of a dry morning: parallel threads the length of a sand lane, the pegs, two people walking the line, roofs and palms on either side. The shot the film is built on, and one that only exists on the mornings a warp is laid.
The same warp at ground level along its length, and the cross made at the far peg.
A bobbin filling on a hand winder, close and long.
Size worked into the warp by hand along its length.
The beam wound tooth by tooth with somebody holding the tension.
The threading, filmed long and in few cuts: the low chair, the wire hook, one end at a time through a heddle eye and then one dent of the reed, with the duration left intact.
The loom made ready out of sequence: wedges tapped under the frame until it stands level, the treadles tried, the floor swept.
Four sheds in one sequence, four reeds of different counts, four setts and patterns, four people, and one reed held close with the dents counted along an inch.
The tying-in: old ends knotted to new in bunches, knots drawn through the reed, the beam tensioned.
The first treadle, the first pick, and the first visibly rough inches of cloth.
The first metre held up against the window, a crossed end traced back, a missed dent found and corrected, and the list of faults that will stay for the whole warp.
The loom simply running, held very long, with nobody watching it and the shed's ordinary noise.
The village from height at last light, with the lane empty and swept and the peg holes still in the sand.
The warp beam at the end of the day, with its diameter visibly smaller than in the morning.
suggested_location.access: By road south from the district town, then into sand lanes and private compounds. Everything depends on the households, because the looms are in people's homes and the most intimate material in the film is somebody's front room; the way in is through a producer group or a weavers' society the households already belong to, or through the state handloom and small-industries offices, rather than cold. Nothing about the schedule is in the film's control: a warp is laid when a warp runs out, which cannot be arranged, so the crew has to be able to arrive on short notice and to stay for the week that follows. Drone flight over the lane and over occupied compounds needs the agreement of the houses underneath whatever the general rules allow, and the lanes are narrow enough that low flying is not appropriate. There is no restricted-access problem here of the kind the far north has, but this is a district with a heavy recent history and a crew should be clear with everybody about what the film is and is not.
suggested_location.best_time: A dry, still stretch, and a working week rather than a day, timed against a household's own warp running out. The outdoor warping has to be caught on the morning it happens, which means being in the village before it and waiting. The threading is filmed across whatever days it actually takes. One short return visit weeks later, to film the same loom still running on the same warp with the beam much smaller, would give the film its one measure of the length of ordinary work.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, and unverified on the ground. From the sources above: this district has handloom weaving artisans of its own; a village reported at about thirteen kilometres from the district town is substantially engaged in handloom production, with both men and women weaving and many of them working from their own homes, producing sarongs, saris, table linen and small goods; there are registered handloom producers in the district; and there is a national handloom training centre that teaches textile design to weavers. The coordinates are the published position of the nearest town on the coast road south of the district town and are a direction towards the kind of village the film needs rather than a survey: no household, shed, loom, group or weaver has been identified or approached, and no permission of any kind has been sought. The technical sequence assumed here — bobbin winding, a warp of several hundred metres laid outdoors between pegs and crossed at the far end, sizing, beaming, drawing each end through a heddle and then a dent of the reed over about three days, tying in to the ends of the previous warp, and a first rough hand's width of cloth — is general handloom practice and is not confirmed for this district; the number of ends, the length of the warp, the time the threading takes and whether the new warp is tied in rather than threaded from scratch are all the first things to check, and the film's proportion depends on them. The local term recorded above for the reed is reported and not confirmed. No photograph of this district's sheds, of an outdoor warping, of a threading or of any part of this work was found on Wikimedia Commons; the one image is of a handloom weaver photographed elsewhere in the country.

unknowns: Whether warps are still laid outdoors in the lanes here, which is the film's single most important shot and its reason for being in this place at all.
Whether a whole setting-up — winding, warping, sizing, beaming, threading, tying in and the first picks — still happens within one village, or whether the preparation has moved to a central facility.
How long the threading actually takes on these looms and how many ends are involved, since the film's whole proportion rests on the answer.
Whether a new warp is tied in to the old ends or threaded from scratch, which changes the film's decisive beat.
Whether a household will allow the work in its own front room to be filmed over a week without the pace or the order being adjusted, and while its earnings and orders stay off screen.
Whether a warp running out can be known about far enough ahead for a crew to be there for the morning the next one is laid.

Whether height can be obtained over the lanes and compounds with the agreement of the houses underneath, and whether the laid warp reads from directly above as strongly as it appears to from the ground.
